newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president seen as would-be dictator.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president seen as would-be dictator.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, locked in a constitutional row which sharply escalated on Friday, is a master of populist rhetoric who has promised Belarus union with Russia and a fight against corruption.
But his opponents say he is a would-be dictator for pushing on with a November 24 referendum which would extend his term and tighten his grip on all branches of power.
The developing crisis in Belarus is being compared to the run-up to a bloody conflict in Russia in 1993, which President Boris Yeltsin ended by sending tanks against parliament.

But Lukashenko has some experience of his own of such stand-offs. Last year he ordered police to evict several liberal deputies who went on hunger strike to protest against his policies. They were beaten by police in the chamber.
Communists, liberals and nationalists have joined forces to oppose Lukashenko and his authoritarian style of rule.
But there is a lack of strong opposition leadership in this nation of 10 million sandwiched between Russia and Poland.

Lukashenko's parliamentary opponents compare him to World War Two dictators Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini. Last year Lukashenko himself in an interview with a German newspaper praised Hitler for his strong rule in pre-war Germany.

Lukashenko, 42, was born in the village of Kopys in eastern Belarus. In Soviet days he was a "politruk" or political instructor in the Soviet Army, a low-level activist in the Komsomol youth organisation and then took over a state farm.
He began his rise to power as the head of parliament's anti-corruption commission, winning the presidency by a landslide in July 1994.

His sensational statements about high-level corruption brought him political glory and popularity among impoverished Belarussians, and his policy of forming a union with Russia struck a chord with a nation struggling to define itself.
Belarussians' national identity was all but crushed under tsarist and Soviet rule. They almost lost their language, to the extent that only a small percentage still speak it well.
For a few months after the vote he distanced himself from Moscow, saying: "Let's stop playing the Russian card."
But as economic crisis deepened, he renewed his pro-Russian rhetoric. Last April he and Russian President Boris Yeltsin signed a pact forming a community.
Lukashenko introduced a small measure of market reform to the economy at first, but reforms have since ground almost to a halt and international lending bodies have suspended credits.

"Lukashenko's personal ambitions... gave him a feeling of claustrophobia on Belarus's political stage. He dreams of playing on the Russian one," the Moscow daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta wrote this week. "It's a pity that his bad performance is killing a good idea (of Russian-Belarussian unity)."
Lukashenko regularly ignores the constitution and Belarussian law, and he has kept tight controls on the media.

There is no strong opposition party and no independent media in Belarus. Lukashenko banned independent trade unions, sacked newspaper editors and closed radio stations. He even threatened this week to expel two Russian television journalists.

He shows open nostalgia for the Soviet Union, and pushed through a decision at a referendum in May 1995 to replace new state symbols with Soviet-style ones. But he now favours Orthodoxy rather than Marxism-Leninism.

Lukashenko, who has described NATO as a "dreadful monster", has made no moves to shift 18 strategic nuclear missiles he is supposed to send for destruction to Russia by the end of the year in line with the START-1 arms reduction treaty.

Last year, after his forces shot down an air balloon killing two American pilots taking part in an international race, Lukashenko appologised and then praised his military for their "high level of readiness."
Belarus is the only European state outside former Yugoslavia which has yet to join the Council of Europe and has been regularly accused by human rights watchdogs of abuses.
